 If it isn’t strange enough for a young European athlete to realize that taking classes is required to play basketball at U.S. colleges, imagine what Motiejus Krivas and his fellow international NCAA players must be thinking now.
 A court order is also needed in many cases now, too.
 Like the one that Krivas’ potential Arizona frontcourt mate, Clemson transfer RJ Godfrey, has been scheduled to pursue during a hearing scheduled for Tuesday at Pima County Superior Court with Judge Jeffrey Bergin. It’s Godfrey’s third legal attempt to get eligible as a fifth-year player this season, after he hit roadblocks in five-for-five cases in Georgia and Texas.
 All European players normally have to do to play high-level basketball in their home continent is sign a contract with a club, maybe develop first with its junior outfit and aim for a promotion to the top level.

 Classes, if desired, can be arranged elsewhere. And legal maneuvers don’t appear routinely necessary.
 “It is weird, yeah, but we can’t control it,” Krivas said of the many lawsuits around college sports. “We just have to focus on our team.”
 Krivas said he was “100 percent” convinced that Godfrey will gain eligibility somehow, which is a reasonable assumption to make considering how most five-for-five players have gained eligibility via court orders in other states.
 Godfrey is actually the only one of 21 Big 12 “five for five” players who hasn’t gained eligibility via a court order, according to Sports Illustrated’s tracker, while former Saint Louis star Robbie Avila just jumped over to the league when he received five-for-five clearance but not a Saint Louis roster spot and signed with TCU.
 Arizona forward RJ Godfrey prepares to react to a Wildcat three in the second half against NAU at McKale Center on Nov. 10, 2026.
 Grace Trejo
 Initially, Godfrey was a winner, gaining eligibility via his Georgia five-for-five case in August, one of many plaintiffs there to receive a temporary restraining order that would have allowed him eligibility — until the Georgia Court of Appeals in September granted the NCAA a stay on that order.
 Last month, Godfrey jumped into a Texas five-for-five case, but that went nowhere when a Texas District Judge ruled just as the season opened that plaintiffs who joined from other jurisdictions would not receive injunctive relief.
 So then Godfrey turned earlier this month to Pima County, where Tucson attorney Ali Farhang and Puerto Rico-based counsel Ryan Downton filed an unusual five-for-five lawsuit on Godfrey’s behalf that named UA and the Arizona Board of Regents as defendants, but not the NCAA.
 The lawsuit was an attention-getting move because it has the potential to help both the plaintiff (Godfrey) and the defendant (UA) — since a court order would basically force UA to certify one of its potentially best players. 
 Godfrey’s attorneys are arguing that UA has been “breaching its obligations” by failing to certify Godfrey when the NCAA Manual does not specify an exclusion for 2022 high school graduates such as Godfrey from its Bylaw 12.6 that allows athletes an unrestricted five-year window of eligibility starting on their 19th birthday or enrollment in college, whichever comes first.
 “Under the plain text of Bylaw 12.6, he is eligible to compete in 2026-27,” Godfrey’s attorneys wrote in their initial complaint.
 During a scheduling hearing last week in Pima County Superior Court, UA's Phoenix-based outside counsel, Brendan Melander, told Bergin the NCAA was not part of the lawsuit and that the organization is in charge of enforcing its eligibility rules. The NCAA has the option to join UA as a defendant if it wants to.
 According to Boise State law professor Sam Ehrlich, who has been closely following five-for-five cases across the country, some five-for-five plaintiffs have added their schools as a defendant along with the NCAA but said Godfrey’s appears to be the only lawsuit that just names the school as a defendant.
 Godfrey’s attorneys said the NCAA passed on opportunities to write in a 2022 exception to its five-on-five rule in its Manual, instead relying on notes, press releases and website guidance to say those players are not eligible.
 Under the NCAA’s old eligibility rules, players had a maximum of four years to compete within a five-year window, so it has argued that 2022 high school graduates who have already played four years of college sports exhausted their eligibility before the new rule went into effect last summer.
 Godfrey’s attorneys said they asked UA to formally certify Godfrey on Nov. 2, the day the college basketball season opened, but were told that the NCAA directed schools not to certify any class of 2022 player who had played four years.
 Among the exhibits from Godfrey's attorneys is a letter from Kristen Arquilla, UA's senior associate AD for compliance, saying that Godfrey is not eligible because the NCAA directed "through an Ed Column" that 2022 players are not eligible under the new five-for-five rule.
 “The University’s refusal thus does not rest on any provision of the Manual,” the complaint read. “It reasons solely on the NCAA’s extratextual directive and threats, and the University has represented that it will certify Godfrey upon a court order establishing his eligibility.”
 The wording of a possible court order is also key. Even if Bergin grants Godfrey a temporary restraining order and/or a preliminary injunction, UA might not certify him unless there is clear language preventing the school from being retroactively penalized by the NCAA for playing Godfrey in the event that the ruling is later overturned. 
 UA indicated it was taking a conservative approach in August: The school did not clear Godfrey to play exhibition games for the Wildcats in Lithuania that month, even though at that time he had a court order from Georgia, but not wording that specified UA could not be penalized.
 Attorneys for both sides had until Monday to submit additional filings in advance of Tuesday's hearing, while it was possible Godfrey and/or other UA basketball notables could be called as witnesses to appear in Tuesday’s hearing.
 In their initial complaint, Godfrey’s attorneys went on to cite other five-for-five cases, noting that over 300 members of the high school class of 2022 have received court orders allowing them to play in 2026-27.
 Maybe Godfrey will become the next, potentially becoming eligible in time to play Wednesday against UConn. The Wildcats have a clear need for his physical, high-motor game and are expected to plug him in immediately as a starting power forward if they can.
 Krivas was already looking forward to such a possibility after the Wildcats beat Auburn last Friday.
 “I know it will happen,” Krivas said. “It’s just a matter of time. We wish we had RJ. He’s a super experienced guy, and he shows his experience in practice.
 "He goes hard. He sacrifices himself in practice as (by behaving like) another team’s player and then on the bench he’s such a supportive guy. He sees the game in his own way. He gives examples, advice. It’s really fortunate to have.”
